meta_title: SSL/TLS Certificates in VpnHood! MANAGER | VpnHood!
meta_description: Use your own domain in VpnHood! MANAGER with a Let's Encrypt certificate it renews by itself, and see which certificate the access keys carry and what each setting does.
title: SSL/TLS certificates
lead: Your servers present a certificate at the start of every connection, and the access keys of a server farm name one of its certificates. MANAGER makes one for every new farm, and can get a trusted one from Let's Encrypt and renew it by itself.
where_card: Open [manager_server_farms] and then the farm: its [manager_certificates] lists them, and a flag marks the one the farm's keys carry. The list's title opens the full list, which adds each certificate's [manager_mode] and [manager_priority].
shot_card_alt: The SSL / TLS Certificates of a server farm in VpnHood! MANAGER, with one certificate, marked with a flag
shot_card_caption: A new farm's certificate: self-signed, with a made-up name, and in the keys.
where_new: Every new farm gets one: a self-signed certificate with a made-up name, which its keys carry until you choose another.
where_server: A server's own page has the same list, with only the certificates that server uses alone.
domain_intro: To have the farm's keys carry your own domain, with a trusted certificate from Let's Encrypt, you need:
domain_req_name: A domain or a subdomain you control, such as [domain_example]. Use a single name, not a wildcard, and one that does not say VPN: apps send it in clear at the start of every connection, where the network can read it.
domain_req_dns: A DNS record that points it straight at one of the farm's servers: an A record, and an AAAA record if the server has an IPv6 address. To put Cloudflare in front of the server, finish these steps first, then turn its proxy on.
domain_req_port: TCP port [port_http] open on that server for as long as you use the domain: the certificate is checked through it, and renewed through it every few months.
domain_add: Open [manager_server_farms] and then the farm, not a server's own page: a certificate added there belongs to that one server. Under [manager_certificates], select [manager_add], enter the domain as [manager_domain_name] and select [manager_create]. MANAGER creates a self-signed certificate for it and opens it.
domain_autosign: Edit [manager_signing] and choose [manager_autosign]. MANAGER asks Let's Encrypt for a certificate, which checks the domain through your server on TCP port [port_http].
domain_signed: Wait until [manager_signature] reads [manager_ca_signed]. From then on, MANAGER renews the certificate by itself before it expires.
domain_token: Edit [manager_visibility] and choose [manager_public_in_token]. Every key of the farm now carries the domain, and the farm's previous certificate becomes [manager_public].
shot_domain_alt: A certificate for server1.example.com in VpnHood! MANAGER, set up as these steps describe: Signing AutoSign (1), Signature CA Signed (2) and Visibility PublicInToken (3)
shot_domain_caption: The domain's certificate when it is done: signed by Let's Encrypt, and carried in every key of the farm.
domain_keys: Keys you copy from MANAGER from now on carry the domain. Apps holding an older key get the new one when they connect, as [manager_push_token] is on by default. Keep the farm's previous certificate until then: older keys work only while it is there.
domain_failed: If the check fails, fix the DNS record or open the port: AutoSign, below, says how MANAGER tries again.
domain_check: To check, open the farm: under [manager_access_points], the domain comes first.
settings_open: Select a certificate's domain to open it.
shot_dialog_alt: A certificate in VpnHood! MANAGER, with its Visibility, Signing, Used By, Priority and Signature
shot_dialog_caption: The certificate MANAGER made for a new farm.
set_visibility: [manager_visibility] decides who gets the certificate's domain. [manager_public_in_token] puts it in every key of the farm; only one certificate can have it, and giving it to another makes this one [manager_public]. A [manager_public] certificate that one server uses alone, if it is [manager_ca_signed], reaches apps only when MANAGER sends them to that server. A [manager_private] one never does. Whatever you choose, servers present the certificate to apps that ask for its domain.
set_signing: [manager_signing] decides how it gets signed. [manager_manual] leaves it as it is. [manager_autosign] has Let's Encrypt sign it and MANAGER renew it, as below. [manager_domain_only] is for a domain whose certificate lives elsewhere: MANAGER never puts it on servers, and keys cannot carry it.
set_used_by: [manager_used_by] is [manager_server_farm], for every server of the farm, or one of its servers. Keep the certificate in the keys on [manager_server_farm], so every server can present it to the apps that hold them.
set_priority: [manager_priority], [manager_priority_normal], [manager_priority_low] or [manager_priority_lowest], orders the domains of [manager_public] certificates when MANAGER gives apps several. It does not change which certificate a server presents.
set_signature: [manager_signature] reads [manager_ca_signed] when a certificate authority signed it, and [manager_self_signed] otherwise. Apps check a [manager_ca_signed] certificate the way a browser does, by its authority and its name, so their keys keep working when it is renewed. A [manager_self_signed] one they accept only by the fingerprint in their key.
set_description: [manager_description] is a note for you. MANAGER does not use it.
add_how: Under [manager_certificates], select [manager_add], enter a [manager_domain_name] and select [manager_create]. MANAGER creates a self-signed certificate for the domain, [manager_public] and [manager_manual], and opens it. The other fields only fill in the certificate's details.
add_server: Added from a server's own page, the certificate is used by that server alone.
add_trusted: To have a certificate authority sign it, set [manager_signing] to [manager_autosign]. Use your own domain, above, walks through that, and through putting the domain in the keys.
autosign_how: With [manager_autosign], MANAGER asks Let's Encrypt to sign a certificate for the domain. Let's Encrypt checks the domain over plain HTTP on TCP port [port_http], so the domain must point at one of the farm's servers, with that port open. MANAGER checks the same way first. Meanwhile, [manager_signing] shows [manager_validating].
autosign_renew: About 30 days before the certificate expires, MANAGER renews it. Let's Encrypt's certificates last 90 days.
autosign_failed: If a check fails, [manager_signing] shows why, in red. MANAGER tries again about once a day, and after six failures in a row it sets [manager_signing] back to [manager_manual]. To try again at once, choose [manager_manual] and then [manager_autosign].
upload_how: [manager_upload] takes a certificate you got elsewhere: a PFX file with its private key, which must be exportable, and its [manager_certificate_password]. Choose its [manager_visibility] as you upload it; it starts at [manager_private]. [manager_signature] reads [manager_ca_signed] if MANAGER can verify who signed it.
upload_farm: An uploaded certificate is used by the whole farm, even when you upload it from a server's page. To give it to one server, change its [manager_used_by] afterwards.
keys_carry: The farm's keys carry the domain of its [manager_public_in_token] certificate, and its fingerprint. If it is [manager_ca_signed], apps look the domain up and accept any certificate an authority signed for it. If it is [manager_self_signed], they accept only that certificate, and they need a server's address to reach it: MANAGER then requires one of the farm's servers to have a [manager_public_in_token] address.
keys_change: Giving [manager_public_in_token] to another certificate leaves the old one on the servers as [manager_public], so older keys keep connecting. Apps get the new key when they connect, as [manager_push_token] is on by default.
keys_replace: Adding or uploading a certificate for a domain the farm already has replaces the old one, which is deleted. The new one keeps the old one's [manager_visibility] if that was higher, so a renewal stays in the keys. Older keys keep working if the new certificate is [manager_ca_signed]. If it is self-signed, give your users new keys.
delete_rules: Select [manager_delete] in its dialog. MANAGER does not let you delete the certificate in the keys, or the farm's last certificate used by the whole farm: give [manager_public_in_token] to another certificate, or add one, first.
next_access_points: Set the addresses your servers listen on and put in their keys
next_proxy: Put your server behind a reverse proxy
